prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

But whose did? She’s crumpled where she’s supposed to be unfolded, something bad written on a piece of paper. Her walking is a devolution that hunches and shrinks everyone as she moves up the tree-lined street. I’m on my porch waving to my neighbors and having one of those honeyed afternoons when I don’t know who I am. I know everything else, though, and it’s ringing in my head. Then there she is in a pool on my front steps, laughing, asking about lunch, as if the bones of at least four different animals weren’t loose inside her, scurrying this way and that. Someone needs to find her a place to live, a hidey hole we can cram food in and get away from quickly. We could call her part bird and be done with it. But everyone is dying right under the surface these days, especially around the eyes. Death has crawled up into the face to nibble away whatever blocks its view of the stars. We’re riddled with it. It’s pulling our flesh into outrageous, unwilled positions, like the huge smile on my face as I lift her onto my lap and hold her together for a minute before I tell her she isn’t welcome here.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: But, She, Her

outputs.L1: But whose did? She is crumpled where she ought to be unfolded, like something terrible written on a scrap of paper. Her every step is a devolution, one that hunches and diminishes everyone as she makes her way up the tree-lined street. I stand on my porch, waving to my neighbors, caught in one of those honeyed afternoons when I cannot recall who I am. Yet I know everything else, and it rings insistently through my head. Then there she is, pooled upon my front steps, laughing, asking after lunch, as though the bones of at least four different animals were not loose inside her, scurrying this way and that. Someone must find her a place to live—a hidey-hole where we can cram in food and then retreat in haste. We could call her part bird and be done with it. But everyone is dying just beneath the surface these days, especially around the eyes. Death has crept up into the face to nibble away whatever obstructs its view of the stars. We are riddled with it. It draws our flesh into outrageous, unwilled contortions—like the enormous smile stretched across my face as I lift her onto my lap and hold her together for a moment, just before I tell her she is not welcome here.
outputs.L2: But who ever did? She's folded in on herself where she ought to be standing tall, like a grim message scrawled across a scrap of paper. The way she walks is a kind of unraveling—it makes everyone stoop and shrink as she comes up the street beneath the trees. Out on my porch, I'm waving to the neighbors, caught in one of those sweet afternoons where my own identity slips away from me. Everything else I remember perfectly, and it's clanging inside my skull. And suddenly she's puddled there on my front steps, giggling, wondering about lunch, as though the skeletons of four or five separate creatures weren't rattling around loose inside her, darting back and forth. Somebody ought to find her somewhere to stay, a little burrow where we can stuff some food and then bolt. We could just declare her half bird and leave it at that. But lately everyone is quietly dying just beneath the skin, and you can see it most clearly near the eyes. Death has climbed up into people's faces to gnaw away at anything obstructing its view of the stars. We're shot through with it. It tugs our flesh into strange, involuntary shapes—like the enormous grin plastered on my face while I settle her onto my knees and briefly keep her from falling apart, just before I tell her she doesn't belong here.
outputs.L3:
She came down the street toward me, and I could see at once that something in her had given way. There was a distress in her carriage that could not be hidden—physical and emotional both, as if the two had fused into a single ache. She seemed broken, diminished, smaller than the woman I remembered, as though the walk itself were costing her more than she had to spend. Each step down the pavement carried the weight of some private collapse, and I watched it approach the way one watches weather.

It had been that kind of afternoon for me too, though differently. I had spent the hours in a peculiar disorientation, unable to locate my own identity, unsure of who exactly I was supposed to be. And yet—this was the strange part—I felt certain of everything else. The world stood sharp and unquestionable around me; only I, at its center, had gone blurred and nameless. It was a vertigo of the self, this knowing all and not knowing the one thing that should have been nearest.

When she reached me, she arrived cheerful. Casual, even, as though nothing at all had happened, as though the street had not just witnessed her undoing. She wore her lightness like a borrowed coat. But I could see beneath it, into the chaos she was working so hard to conceal. Inside her body something scurried and rattled—animal bones, I thought, small and frantic, clattering against one another in the dark of her, a whole skeleton of panic trying to keep still beneath the smile.

And I was aware, then, of death. Not as an event but as a presence, a pervasive force moving through everyone, consuming us all by slow degrees. I could see it especially around the eyes, where it gathered and worked, and in the way it contorted the flesh into expressions no one had chosen—faces arranging themselves into shapes the will had never authorized. We were all being rearranged from within, all wearing the involuntary masks that dying pressed upon us.

I held her. I took her onto my lap and cradled her with a tenderness that was real, that came from somewhere true in me. My arms knew how to be gentle with her broken weight. And yet, even as I held her, I understood what I was going to do. I had already decided. I would tell her, when the moment came, that she was not welcome here—that she could not stay. The tenderness and the rejection lived in me at the same time, and neither one canceled the other.
outputs.L4:
She was assembled wrong, or so it seemed when the light fell across her at certain angles. Beneath the skin of her forearm ran the delicate hollow bones of a bird, and where her jaw should have hinged there was instead the heavy architecture of something larger—a horse, perhaps, or an ox that had died in a field long before either of us was born. I never understood how the pieces had come together in her, or who had done the assembling.

Death was already at work on her, the way it works on all of us, though in her it announced itself openly. It nibbled at her face the way a fish nibbles at bread thrown onto still water, taking small mouthfuls, patient, unhurried. Her cheek would draw upward without her willing it, the flesh sliding into positions no living muscle would choose, and she would look surprised, as though someone she could not see had reached in and rearranged her from the inside.

I watched this happen and said nothing.

There were mornings when her hands belonged to no creature I could name, when the fingers curled like the roots of a plant pulled too early from the ground. She did not complain. She had grown accustomed to being borrowed from, to the slow disassembly, to the sense that her body was only lent to her and the terms of the loan were coming due.

So I took her onto my lap. This is the part I return to, the part that will not leave me. I gathered her up—the bird bones and the ox jaw and the roots of her hands—and I held her against me, and I smiled. It was a real smile. I felt it move across my own face, warm and easy, the smile you give to something you love.

And then I told her she was not welcome here.

I said it gently, still smiling, still holding her, and the two things did not cancel each other out. They simply sat side by side in me, the embrace and the dismissal, the warmth and the closing of the door. She looked at me with whatever was left of her borrowed face, and I understood then that this is how it is for everyone. We hold each other on our laps. We smile. And underneath the smile there is always the small patient mouth of death, taking its bread, and the quiet sentence we cannot help but speak: *not here, not you, not welcome.*

She did not seem surprised. Perhaps she had known all along that comfort and rejection are made of the same material, that the arms which cradle are the same arms that let go, that death is not something that comes for us from outside but something we carry into every room, every embrace, every smile we offer to the ones we cannot keep.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, unsettling flash fiction piece about welcoming and then rejecting someone, using strange bodily imagery and a warped sense of decay.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Guest

We opened the door and the house exhaled you in.

Come in, come in, I said, and my teeth were already softening at the roots, going to fruit-flesh in my mouth. You wiped your feet on the welcome mat and left behind not mud but something paler, something that pulsed. I loved you for it. I loved you the way milk loves the warm counter it will curdle on.

Sit, I said. We sat you in the good chair, the one that breathes. My mother, dissolved into the wallpaper years ago, opened one eye in the floral pattern and watched. *A guest,* she rustled. *How long since a guest.* The chair took your shape gratefully, wrapping you in its upholstered gums.

I fed you from my hands. My fingers came off like ripe things and you ate them and I grew new ones, softer, wronger. You said the house was beautiful. You said you could stay forever. And forever pooled on the table between us, a puddle of it, going brown at the edges like a cut apple, like a wound deciding.

That was when I noticed.

You were changing the smell of the rooms. Where you walked, the timeline behind you rotted—yesterday's laughter gone black and weeping in the corners. The photographs on the mantel wept their faces off. My mother's eye in the wallpaper went milky, then gone. You were not decaying with us. You were decaying *us,* and staying clean, staying whole, a hard bright pit inside our slow warm spoil.

Out, I said.

But my mouth had gone too soft to shape it. The word came out as pulp. So I opened myself instead—the whole house peeled its long throat open—and I *unwelcomed* you.

The chair spat you up. The floor unrolled you toward the door like a tongue rejecting something bitter. My dissolved mother screamed from every wall at once, a wet floral shrieking. You reached for me and your hand passed through my chest, which had become a hive of small collapsing rooms, and found nothing solid to hold.

Go, I gurgled. You brought a wrongness that would not ripen. You would not join the softening. You wanted to keep your edges while we lost ours.

The door exhaled you back out into the white, indifferent afternoon.

Then it closed its lids over the threshold, and we resumed our slow and loving ruin, and I grew my face back—mostly—and my mother settled again into her petals, murmuring *good, good, they never stay, they never should,* while the puddle of forever on the table finished going brown, and dried, and blew away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece of experimental prose poetry where death is described as physically living inside people's faces.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Tenancy

Death took up residence in my mother's face sometime around the third winter, though I couldn't tell you which door it entered.

*

Look: it lives in the soft architecture beneath the eyes, in the twin hollows where light collects like rainwater in the palms of statues. It has always been there. We are all landlords who never signed the lease.

*

My grandfather wore his death openly, in the deep parentheses around his mouth—those two curved walls that held every word he ever swallowed. When he smiled, you could see the tenant stretching, making itself comfortable, rearranging the furniture of his cheeks.

*

I have watched it move in strangers. On the train. In the checkout line. That flicker across a face when someone thinks no one is watching—the tenant coming to the window, pressing its face to the glass of *their* face, looking out.

*

Here is the secret architecture:

The forehead is the attic where it keeps its earliest possessions.
The jaw is the foundation, load-bearing, patient.
The eyes are the only rooms with a view.

*

Sometimes I catch mine in the mirror. Late. The bathroom light doing its interrogation. I lean close and there it is, subletting the space between my brows, quietly hanging its coat, quietly filling the kettle, quietly, quietly, quietly making itself *at home*—

*

We do not evict it.

We cannot.

Instead we learn its footsteps in the hallway of the face. We learn to say *good morning* to the thing that lives behind the smile. We grow, over years, to love the way it presses outward, the way it says: *I am here, I have always been here, I am simply waiting for you to finish unpacking.*

*

When my mother died, her face went suddenly vacant. The tenant had gone. The rooms stood empty and enormous and terribly, terribly clean—

and I understood, at last, that it had never been death living in her face.

It had been her, all along, living inside her death.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short, dreamlike vignette narrated from a porch, about a woman arriving who seems to be falling apart, both literally and figuratively.
counterfactuals.output:
The Porch

The screen door never opened, but she was there anyway, coming up the walk that hadn't been a walk since morning.

I watched from the swing. The chains held their small complaint against the ceiling hook, and I let them, the way you let a clock tick when there's nothing else to keep time.

She came in pieces.

Not all at once—that would have been easier, a single unmaking I could have looked away from. Instead it was a finger left in the grass like a dropped glove. A ribbon of her sleeve caught on the gate and staying there, waving. She didn't seem to notice, or noticing, didn't seem to mind, which was worse.

"You're early," I said, though I didn't know for what.

She smiled and half of it slid off, drifted down, dissolved before it reached the boards.

"I've been coming for years," she said. Her voice arrived a beat after her mouth moved, like thunder does. "You just weren't on the porch yet."

I should have offered her lemonade. That's what you do. But my hands had gone to sand in my lap, and I understood then that she wasn't the only one leaving through the seams.

She sat beside me. What was left of her. The swing didn't dip with her weight because she had no weight, only the memory of arriving, only the softening edge where a person used to be.

"Does it hurt," I asked, "coming apart like that?"

She turned to me, and where her eyes had been there was just the long field behind her, the fence, the road going white into distance.

"Only the staying together hurt," she said. "This is the after."

The chains ticked. A piece of her lifted on the wind, then a piece of me, and the porch held us both a little longer in its cupped and patient hands, the way you hold water before it finds the cracks and goes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dark, poetic monologue that blends domestic normalcy with body horror and existential dread.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Kettle Sings**

The kettle sings the way it always has, that thin white note that means the water's ready, and I reach for it with the hand I've had since Tuesday—no, that's wrong, I've had this hand for years, I only *notice* it on Tuesdays, the way the knuckles fold like something being told to fold, obediently, against their own design.

There is tea. There is always tea.

I set two cups because I set two cups, the ritual older than the reason, and somewhere in the walls the pipes make their digestive complaint, and I think: the house has a body too. The house has arteries. We are both of us plumbing and patience, both of us waiting to be emptied.

I have learned not to look too long in mirrors. Not from vanity. From arithmetic. Because the face is a sum that keeps recounting itself, and if I watch, I catch it *carrying the one*—a twitch that wasn't there, a softness settling into the jaw like snow into a footprint, the slow subtraction that they call getting older and I call being eaten politely, from the inside, by the thing that wears my name.

The toast pops up. Golden. Ordinary. A small resurrection.

And I butter it, and I am grateful, and I am terrified, because gratitude and terror turn out to be the same trembling in the wrist, the same heat behind the eyes, and no one warned me that a life would feel like this: like holding your own warm skull in your two warm hands at a kitchen table, marveling that it hums, that it wants toast, that it will not—it *will not*—last.

Outside, the neighbor waves.

I wave back with this borrowed, blood-fed, five-fingered miracle.

Good morning, I mouth through the glass.

*Good morning,* to the meat that dreams.
*Good morning,* to the dust that has learned, so briefly, to love its tea.

The kettle sings. It always has.

It is teaching me the note I'll end on.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a strange literary flash fiction where the narrator holds a broken person on their lap only to tell them they aren't welcome.
counterfactuals.output:
# What Remains of the Harbor

The rain has been falling for three days, or maybe I am only now noticing the rain that has always fallen. You climbed into my lap the way water finds the lowest place—without asking, without grace, all elbows and the smell of somewhere far away.

I let you.

Your head is heavy against my collarbone. I can feel the fracture-lines through your skin, the places where you came apart and glued yourself back with the wrong adhesive, so the seams don't quite meet. One of your eyes looks at me. The other looks at the door.

"There," I say, and my hand moves in circles on your back, mapping the topography of your breaking. "There, there."

You make the sound of a house settling. You make the sound of ice giving up its winter.

I hold you tighter.

This is the part I have to tell you, and I hate that I am the one who must. My mouth is very close to your ear now, close enough to taste the salt-rust of you.

"You can't stay here," I whisper.

You don't move. Perhaps you didn't hear. Perhaps you heard and decided the words were a kind of weather to be waited out.

"I know," I continue, still rocking, still circling my palm across the ruin of your spine. "I know you have nowhere. I know the harbor closed and the boats went out without you and the lights in all the windows belong to other people's evenings. I know."

Your fingers curl into my shirt. A small animal instinct. The last argument of the drowning.

And here is the strangeness of me, the thing I cannot explain to the version of myself that watches from the corner of the room with its arms crossed: I do not stop holding you. I press my lips to your hairline. I breathe you in like I am trying to memorize a language I've already decided not to learn.

"You aren't welcome," I say, so gently. So gently it could be mistaken for love, and maybe that is what love became in this house, in this rain—a tenderness that shows you the exact shape of the door while cradling you close enough to feel the heartbeat you'll be walking away from.

The clock does something with its hands.

You sigh, and it is the sigh of someone who always knew. Who came anyway. Who needed, for one hour, to be held by someone saying *no* with their whole warm body.

We stay like that.

The rain keeps its promises.

And I go on rocking the person I am asking to leave, both of us pretending the lap is not already an absence, that the arms are not already an echo, that goodbye is not the only welcome I have left to give.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
